blocks.heading: Segmenting and choosing a target
blocks.text: Market segmentation divides a market into groups of consumers with similar needs. The syllabus bases include product, region, purpose, price, age and gender. Segments can overlap: buyers in one region can also seek budget-priced products for a particular purpose. Use evidence that the chosen grouping affects needs rather than assuming all people in a demographic category behave alike. Assess potential demand, purchasing ability, competition, reach and whether the business can serve the segment with its resources. A small enterprise may focus on a niche instead of trying to offer everything to everyone, but excessive dependence on a narrow group creates risk. A supported target decision links a real need with an achievable offering and recognises the strongest alternative.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Tula Bags can make durable work bags in small batches. Interviews indicate mechanics need strong tool compartments, while fashion customers want frequent style changes that Tula cannot provide. Targeting work-purpose buyers fits its capability and the stated need better than the fashion alternative. Confirm sufficient paid demand and feasible price before committing; the word mechanic alone does not prove a profitable market.

blocks.heading: Product segmentation
blocks.text: Product segmentation groups a wider market by the type or category of product sought. It can help a supplier focus its range and expertise, but a product label alone does not explain the customer need. Buyers within a category may still differ in price, use and preferred features.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Uta Sports distinguishes buyers seeking footwear from buyers seeking sports equipment. The categories can guide separate ranges and promotion. Further evidence is needed to choose the footwear features and price.

blocks.heading: Regional segmentation
blocks.text: Regional segmentation groups customers by geographical area. Climate, access, travel distance or local demand can make needs differ between areas. The grouping is useful when those differences affect the offering or delivery; it does not prove everyone in one area wants the same thing.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Oha Clothing compares demand for warm outerwear in colder inland areas with demand in warmer locations. Regional evidence can guide stock and delivery, while actual customer data should check the assumed climate-related need.

blocks.heading: Segmentation by purpose
blocks.text: Purpose segmentation groups customers by the use they want from a product. The same broad product can serve school, work, travel or recreation, requiring different features. This can be more informative than a demographic label where function drives the purchase. A buyer can belong to different purpose segments for different occasions.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Teya Bags distinguishes tool-carrying bags from small everyday leisure bags. Strength and internal compartments may matter for tools, while size and style may matter for leisure. Research should confirm those priorities before design.

blocks.heading: Price segmentation
blocks.text: Price segmentation groups demand by price level or willingness and ability to pay, such as budget and premium ranges. The offering must deliver value the group recognises; a higher price label alone does not create superior quality or willing buyers. Low-price demand can require careful cost control, while a premium offer needs credible benefits.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Kira Furniture compares a simple low-priced desk with a more expensive customised range. The budget group may value affordability, but the desk must still meet its basic purpose. Premium customers need a reason to accept the extra price.

blocks.heading: Age segmentation
blocks.text: Age segmentation groups customers by age where life stage or practical needs affect demand. Children’s and adult sizes can differ, but age does not establish every preference or income level. Use a meaningful product link and evidence instead of stereotypes. A buyer may also purchase on behalf of another age group.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Ema Cycles makes smaller cycles for younger riders and larger sizes for adults. Size and safe fit provide a relevant age-related distinction, while price and style still need evidence from riders and purchasing adults.

blocks.heading: Gender segmentation
blocks.text: Gender segmentation groups demand by gender where evidence shows a relevant difference in needs or preferences. It is one possible basis, not an assumption that every product must have separate male and female versions. Many needs are shared and individuals vary within categories. Choose fit, intended use or actual preferences when those explain demand better.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nela Tailoring tests demand for different clothing cuts, asking customers about fit rather than assuming all preferences from gender. Gender-related ranges may help where fit evidence supports them, but actual measurements and preferences remain important. A tool’s function may be better segmented by purpose instead.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Customer focus and segmentation
blocks.text:
Fictional Rena Lunches can supply one reliable weekday meal range. Interviews with nearby workers show demand for quick affordable lunches. Tourists request varied evening menus that Rena currently cannot prepare. The owner compares serving the local work-purpose segment with launching the preferred evening menu without further customer evidence.

a(i) State two ways Rena could identify customer needs. [2]
a(ii) State the starting focus of market orientation and product orientation. [2]
b State two ways a business can meet a stated customer need. [2]
c Explain why purpose is a useful segmentation basis for Rena. [6]
d Evaluate a customer-led weekday offer against launching the owner’s preferred evening menu. [8]

a(i) Interviews and review of customer feedback. a(ii) Identified consumer wants lead market orientation; the producer’s product focus leads product orientation. b Adapt product features and provide suitable access or timing. c Workers’ short breaks create a quick affordable weekday need, while tourist evening meals have different timing and variety requirements. Purpose helps separate these needs and match Rena’s limited range rather than treat all meal buyers alike. d The weekday offer fits both evidence and capability. The evening menu could reach another market but requires variety Rena cannot currently provide and lacks sufficient evidence. Choose the weekday segment, test paid demand and review results. Customer interest alone is not proof of profitable orders.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Customer focus and segmentation
blocks.text:
Fictional Rena Lunches can supply one reliable weekday meal range. Interviews with nearby workers show demand for quick affordable lunches. Tourists request varied evening menus that Rena currently cannot prepare. The owner compares serving the local work-purpose segment with launching the preferred evening menu without further customer evidence.

a Explain how Rena can connect customer evidence with its product and access decisions. [8]
b Evaluate the proposed target segment against the alternative given Rena’s resources. [12]

a Interviews identify quick affordable worker lunches. Rena can choose a feasible meal, price and convenient weekday collection arrangement, then review actual orders. A preference must become paid demand; service speed and food reliability need monitoring. The choice is market led because evidence precedes design, while capability limits which requests can be served. b A work-purpose focus matches the stated need and one-range capacity, potentially supporting repeat weekday orders. It creates dependence on a local group and must cover costs at an affordable price. Tourist evening demand offers another possibility but conflicts with current variety capability. Choose the worker segment while validating volumes and costs; do not stretch into an unsupported range merely because a different market exists. Reconsider if demand or capability changes.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Customer focus and segmentation
blocks.text:
Fictional Tuli Bags can make durable tool bags. Evidence shows enough local tradespeople interested at a feasible price, while a fashion segment requires rapid design changes beyond current capability. It compares work-purpose targeting with fashion targeting. For part (b) only, reliable new evidence shows most local tradespeople will not pay the feasible price, so the previously sufficient work-purpose demand disappears. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate Tuli’s target choice under the original evidence. [12]
b Evaluate that choice after the price evidence changes. Explain whether the original judgement holds. [12]

a Work-purpose segmentation is justified by specific functional needs, feasible-price interest and capability. Fashion targeting does not fit current design resources. Choose a monitored work-bag test rather than produce for everyone. b The changed willingness to pay removes the sufficiency condition. Do not proceed at the same scale merely because the product is durable. Investigate acceptable features, costs or other reachable buyers before committing. Fashion remains beyond capability, so the failure of one target does not automatically make that alternative suitable. Pause and revise the evidence-led offering; customer focus requires responding to the new finding.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Customer focus and segmentation
blocks.text:
Fictional Tuli Bags can make durable tool bags. Evidence shows enough local tradespeople interested at a feasible price, while a fashion segment requires rapid design changes beyond current capability. It compares work-purpose targeting with fashion targeting.

Evaluate Tuli’s work-purpose target against the fashion alternative under the original facts. Give a concise plan. [12]

Needs and fit: durable tool bags match tradespeople and existing capability. Evidence: sufficient interest at a feasible price must still become purchases. Alternative: fashion requires design changes currently unavailable. Risks: a narrow target creates dependence and preferences can change. Judgement: focus on the evidenced work-purpose segment with a small test and monitoring; avoid assuming a segment name proves success.
